Guest Author

ATLANTA — Artificial intelligence (AI) is everywhere — on our phones, in our inboxes, even proofreading this sentence. Vendors promise transformative gains and revolutionary insights. The need for new technologies is real: despite extensive work from producers and regulators, in 2025, the USDA issued four public health alerts and recalled over 5 million pounds of chicken product.

If AI-equipped inspection, monitoring, and analytics can reduce the frequency of these events, the industry stands to benefit considerably.

For poultry processors, the real opportunity is in targeted, incremental adoption of AI where it strengthens existing food safety systems, not replacing the fundamentals with a cure-all black box solution.

Investment in AI for food safety has accelerated, with startups, equipment manufacturers, and large technology providers entering the space. Approaches range from “smart” equipment and plantwide tools that plug into existing quality assurance programs to general “AI data platforms.”

Processors should ask: Which tools are mature enough for my facility? Where do they fit in my food safety plan? How do they augment my current monitoring practices?

Several near-term applications stand out. AI-driven foreign material detection technologies build on decades of computer vision research. Combining hyperspectral imaging, x-ray, and optical cameras with AI perception models can improve detection of plastics, bone fragments, and other foreign materials. Well-trained systems can adapt to natural product variability and changes in lighting or environment.

Beyond vision, AI models are adept at finding subtle patterns in multimodal data to drive process improvements. Language-based tools can help plants navigate regulations and policies and flag early signs of risk or non-compliance. Imagine securely querying your HACCP plans, regulatory documents, and training materials and getting clear, cited answers tailored for supervisors or new QA staff.

While these applications are promising, they are not plug-and-play solutions. A device being “AI-enabled” does not guarantee it will work robustly, and can pose a risk if applied improperly. Key considerations include data access and ownership, clear objectives, and training of personnel.

Data security is a major concern; many companies have leaked sensitive information through misconfigured AI tools. Retaining legal ownership of your data is not enough if third parties can access or learn from it. Distinguishing between truly local/on-premise tools and cloud-hosted services is critical; that choice can separate responsible AI use from a significant data leak.

Processors should also seek measurable impact from models: How will this tool affect yield, labor efficiency, audit performance, or risk reduction? What problem is it solving and how will you know it is working? No AI model is perfect. AI models are probabilistic and trained from historical data, so processors should maintain well defined fallback procedures to catch new errors and avoid over-reliance on automated decisions.

AI will not disappear; it will only become more capable and embedded in operations as it matures. Producers must understand what these tools can and cannot do and implement safeguards around data, cybersecurity, and governance when using them.

Regulators should work with industry to establish policies and guidelines that both protect consumers and support innovation.

AI technologies can either strengthen food safety or introduce new vulnerabilities. The outcome depends on how they are integrated: clear objectives, alignment with HACCP controls, robust cybersecurity, and a well-trained workforce.

As with any emerging technology, AI should be adopted deliberately, with careful testing and governance, to ensure it serves your organization’s food safety and business goals.

 

Reprinted from PoultryTech, a publication of the Agricultural Technology Research Program of the Georgia Tech Research Institute, a program conducted in cooperation with the Georgia Poultry Federation with funding from the Georgia Legislature. Walker Byrnes is a research engineer with the Georgia Tech Research Institute’s ATRP.

translationZh:
人工智能（AI）无处不在——在我们的手机里、收件箱中，甚至正在校对这句话。供应商承诺带来变革性的收益和革命性的洞察。对新技术的需求是真实存在的：尽管生产者和监管机构付出了大量努力，2025年美国农业部仍发布了四次公共卫生警报，并召回了超过500万磅的鸡肉产品。

如果配备AI的检验、监控和分析工具能够减少这些事件的发生频率，整个行业将受益匪浅。

对于家禽加工企业而言，真正的机遇在于有针对性地、渐进式地采用AI，以强化现有的食品安全体系，而不是用万能的黑匣子解决方案取代基础措施。

对食品安全领域AI的投资正在加速，初创公司、设备制造商和大型技术提供商纷纷进入这一领域。方法从“智能”设备和可接入现有质量保证程序的工厂级工具，到通用的“AI数据平台”不等。

加工企业应自问：哪些工具在我的工厂中已经足够成熟？它们如何融入我的食品安全计划？它们如何增强我当前的监控实践？

几个近期的应用脱颖而出。AI驱动的异物检测技术建立在数十年的计算机视觉研究基础上。将高光谱成像、X射线和光学相机与AI感知模型相结合，可以提高对塑料、骨碎片和其他异物的检测能力。训练有素的系统能够适应自然的产品变异以及光照或环境的变化。

除了视觉，AI模型擅长在多模态数据中发现细微模式，以推动流程改进。基于语言的工具可以帮助工厂理解法规和政策，并标记出风险或不合规的早期迹象。想象一下，安全地查询你的HACCP计划、监管文件和培训材料，并获得针对主管或新QA员工的清晰、有引用的答案。

尽管这些应用前景广阔，但它们并非即插即用的解决方案。设备“具备AI功能”并不能保证其稳健运行，如果应用不当，还可能带来风险。关键考虑因素包括数据访问和所有权、明确的目标以及人员培训。

数据安全是一个主要问题；许多公司因配置不当的AI工具而泄露了敏感信息。如果第三方能够访问或学习你的数据，仅仅保留数据的合法所有权是不够的。区分真正的本地/本地部署工具和云托管服务至关重要；这一选择可能决定负责任的AI使用与重大数据泄露之间的差别。

加工企业还应寻求模型的可衡量影响：该工具将如何影响产量、劳动效率、审计绩效或风险降低？它解决什么问题？你如何知道它在起作用？没有完美的AI模型。AI模型是概率性的，基于历史数据进行训练，因此加工企业应维护明确定义的应急程序，以捕捉新错误，避免对自动化决策的过度依赖。

AI不会消失；随着其成熟，它将变得更加强大并更深入地嵌入运营中。生产者必须了解这些工具能做什么和不能做什么，并在使用它们时实施围绕数据、网络安全和治理的保障措施。

监管机构应与行业合作，制定既保护消费者又支持创新的政策和指南。

AI技术既可以加强食品安全，也可能引入新的漏洞。结果取决于它们如何被整合：明确的目标、与HACCP控制的协调、强大的网络安全以及训练有素的员工队伍。

与任何新兴技术一样，AI应被审慎采用，经过仔细测试和治理，以确保它服务于组织的食品安全和业务目标。
